name: Centaur
first: Clay figurine from Lefkandi, Euboea (c. 900 BCE); named in Homer's Iliad (8th century BCE)
looks: Upper body of a human joined at the waist to the body and four legs of a horse.
habitat: The forested mountains of Thessaly, especially Mount Pelion.
diet: Raw meat and wine — centaurs in myth were wild and easily drunk; the wise Chiron ate like a civilised man.
powers: Great speed and strength; Chiron was a healer, astrologer and teacher of heroes.
stories: Most centaurs were violent: at the wedding of the Lapith king Pirithous they got drunk and tried to carry off the bride, sparking the battle carved on the Parthenon's metopes. Chiron, by contrast, tutored Achilles, Jason, Asclepius and Heracles; wounded by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows, he gave up his immortality and became the constellation Sagittarius (or Centaurus). The centaur Nessus tried to carry off Heracles' wife Deianira and, dying, tricked her with his poisoned blood, which later killed Heracles.
belief: Centaurs symbolised the struggle between civilisation and wild animal nature. Medieval bestiaries and Renaissance art kept them alive; today they appear in C. S. Lewis's Narnia and Harry Potter.
could: Biologically impossible: no vertebrate has six limbs, and a human torso on a horse's body would need two sets of lungs and hearts. A popular theory suggests the myth grew from Greeks first meeting expert horse-riding peoples of the steppe or Thessaly, who seemed to be one with their horses.
verdict: Impossible — but possibly inspired by mounted nomads
connections: Greek religion and mythology; Classical Greece; Heracles; Homer's Iliad (Venetus A); Homer

name: Griffin
first: Seals and art from Susa and Mesopotamia (c. 3000 BCE); Greek accounts from Aristeas of Proconnesus (7th century BCE), retold by Herodotus
looks: Body, tail and hind legs of a lion; head, wings and talons of an eagle.
habitat: The gold-rich mountains of Central Asia (the Altai), far to the north-east of Greece.
diet: Horses and humans who came too close to their gold.
powers: Guardians of treasure and of the divine; incredibly strong flyers.
stories: Herodotus describes one-eyed Arimaspians trying to steal gold from the griffins who guard it in Scythia. Griffins pulled Alexander the Great's flying chariot in medieval romances and appear in Dante's Paradiso pulling a chariot. Gold Scythian art is full of griffins.
belief: As king of beasts and king of birds combined, the griffin became a symbol of power and protection on shields, coats of arms and buildings.
could: No. But folklorist Adrienne Mayor argued in 2000 that Scythian gold-miners in the Gobi and Altai found fossil skeletons of the beaked dinosaur Protoceratops and imagined a beaked, four-legged guardian; palaeontologists have challenged this idea, noting griffin art is older and found far away.
connections: Achaemenid Persian Empire; Scythians; Mesopotamian religion; Alexander the Great; Herodotus

name: Hydra
first: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE)
looks: A giant water serpent with many heads (often nine); one head was immortal.
habitat: The swamps of Lerna near Argos in the Peloponnese, guarding an entrance to the underworld.
diet: Livestock and people of the region; its breath and blood were poisonous.
powers: For every head cut off, two grew back; its blood was a deadly poison.
stories: Killing the Hydra was Heracles' second labour. His nephew Iolaus burned each neck stump with a torch so heads could not regrow, and Heracles buried the immortal head under a rock. He dipped his arrows in its poison — the same poison that later killed the centaurs Chiron and Nessus and, finally, Heracles himself.
belief: 'Hydra-headed' describes problems that multiply when attacked. The constellation Hydra is the largest in the sky.
could: No animal regrows multiple heads. But the tiny freshwater animal named hydra really can regenerate its whole body from small pieces. Some scholars think the myth reflects springs at Lerna that kept bursting out when blocked.
verdict: Impossible — named after by a real regenerating animal
summary: A giant water serpent with many heads (often nine); one head was immortal. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).

name: Medusa and the Gorgons
first: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE); Gorgon faces (gorgoneia) on temples and shields from the 7th century BCE
looks: Women with living snakes for hair, sometimes with tusks, wings and bronze hands; Medusa was the only mortal of the three Gorgon sisters.
habitat: At the edge of the world, beyond the ocean in the far west.
diet: Not described — their danger was their gaze.
powers: Anyone who looked at Medusa's face was turned to stone; even her severed head kept that power.
stories: King Polydectes sent the hero Perseus to fetch Medusa's head. With Athena's polished shield as a mirror, Hermes' winged sandals and Hades' cap of invisibility, Perseus beheaded her while she slept; from her neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor. Perseus used the head to turn the sea monster threatening Andromeda, and later Polydectes, to stone, then gave it to Athena, who placed it on her aegis. In Ovid's later Roman version (8 CE), Medusa was a beautiful priestess punished by Athena after Poseidon assaulted her in Athena's temple — a version many modern writers read as a story of a victim blamed.
belief: Gorgon faces were apotropaic — protective symbols to ward off evil — carved on temples, armour and coins. Medusa appears on the flag of Sicily and the Versace logo, and is now often reclaimed as a symbol of female rage.
could: No creature turns things to stone. The gorgon face may come from older Near Eastern demon masks, or from the frightening faces of predators.
connections: Greek religion and mythology; Perseus; Pegasus; Classical Greece

name: Cyclops
first: Hesiod's Theogony and Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th–7th century BCE)
looks: Giants with a single eye in the middle of the forehead.
habitat: Sicily and remote islands; in Hesiod, they work in forges under volcanoes.
diet: Sheep and goats, cheese and milk — and, in Polyphemus' case, humans.
powers: Immense strength; master smiths who forged Zeus's thunderbolts, Poseidon's trident and Hades' helmet.
stories: In the Odyssey, Odysseus and his men are trapped in the cave of Polyphemus, son of Poseidon, who eats several of them. Odysseus tells him his name is 'Nobody', gets him drunk and blinds him with a burning stake; when Polyphemus cries that 'Nobody' is hurting him, the other Cyclopes ignore him. The men escape clinging under sheep, but Odysseus's boast earns Poseidon's anger and ten years of wandering.
belief: Later Greeks believed Cyclopes built the giant stone walls of Mycenae and Tiryns, which is why such masonry is called 'Cyclopean'.
could: Not as giants. In 1914 palaeontologist Othenio Abel suggested that skulls of extinct dwarf elephants on Mediterranean islands like Sicily and Crete, with a large central nasal opening, looked like a one-eyed giant's skull. Cyclopia, a rare and fatal birth defect, exists in humans and animals but such individuals cannot survive.
verdict: Impossible as giants — likely inspired by elephant fossils
connections: Greek religion and mythology; Odysseus; Homer; Mycenaean Greece; Homer's Iliad (Venetus A)

name: Chimera
first: Homer's Iliad, Book 6 (8th century BCE)
looks: A fire-breathing lion with a goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail.
habitat: The mountains of Lycia in south-west Anatolia.
diet: Livestock and people of Lycia.
powers: Breathes fire.
stories: King Iobates of Lycia sent the hero Bellerophon to kill it, expecting him to die. Riding the winged horse Pegasus, Bellerophon shot it from the air and, in some versions, thrust a lead-tipped spear into its mouth; its fiery breath melted the lead and killed it.
belief: The Etruscan bronze 'Chimera of Arezzo' (c. 400 BCE) is a masterpiece. Today 'chimera' means any impossible hybrid or wild fantasy.
could: No — but at Yanartaş near Olympos in Lycia, natural gas has burned from cracks in the rock for over 2,500 years; ancient writers linked these eternal flames to the Chimera. In biology, real 'chimeras' are organisms containing cells with two different sets of DNA.
verdict: Impossible — possibly inspired by natural gas fires
connections: Greek religion and mythology; Bellerophon; Pegasus; Homer
summary: A fire-breathing lion with a goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail. First attested: Homer's Iliad, Book 6 (8th century BCE).

name: Minotaur
first: Greek vase paintings from the 7th century BCE; myth set in Bronze Age Crete
looks: A man with the head and tail of a bull.
habitat: The Labyrinth built by Daedalus beneath King Minos's palace at Knossos.
diet: Seven young men and seven young women sent from Athens as tribute every year (or nine).
powers: Great strength.
stories: Born to Queen Pasiphaë after Poseidon cursed her to love a bull, the Minotaur was hidden in the Labyrinth. The Athenian prince Theseus volunteered as a tribute; Minos's daughter Ariadne gave him a ball of thread to find his way out. Theseus killed the Minotaur and escaped, but forgot to change his black sails to white, so his father Aegeus threw himself into the sea — the Aegean.
belief: Many historians think the myth reflects Minoan bull worship and the bull-leaping frescoes of Knossos, whose maze-like palace may have suggested the Labyrinth.
could: No.
verdict: Impossible — echo of Minoan bull cults
connections: Minoan civilisation; Greek religion and mythology; Theseus
summary: A man with the head and tail of a bull. First attested: Greek vase paintings from the 7th century BCE; myth set in Bronze Age Crete.

name: Pegasus
first: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE)
looks: A white winged horse.
habitat: Mount Helicon, home of the Muses, and later the stables of Zeus on Olympus.
diet: Like other horses — grass; some say ambrosia.
powers: Flight; where his hoof struck Mount Helicon, the spring Hippocrene burst out, inspiring poets.
stories: Born from the neck of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her, Pegasus was tamed by Bellerophon with a golden bridle from Athena and helped him kill the Chimera. When Bellerophon tried to fly to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus; Bellerophon fell, and Pegasus became a constellation.
belief: A symbol of poetry and inspiration; the emblem of British airborne forces.
could: A horse-sized animal could not fly with feathered wings — it would need enormous flight muscles; the largest flying animals, pterosaurs like Quetzalcoatlus, weighed perhaps 200–250 kg using hollow bones.
connections: Medusa and the Gorgons; Bellerophon; Perseus; Chimera; Greek religion and mythology
summary: A white winged horse. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).

name: Cerberus
first: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE)
looks: A giant dog with three heads (Hesiod says fifty), a serpent tail and snakes growing from its back.
habitat: The gates of the underworld, Hades.
diet: Raw flesh; it devoured those who tried to escape. Sweet honey cakes could distract it.
powers: Prevents the dead from leaving the underworld.
stories: Capturing Cerberus was Heracles' twelfth and final labour; he wrestled it with his bare hands and carried it to King Eurystheus. Orpheus lulled it to sleep with music, and the Sibyl drugged it for Aeneas.
belief: The image of a guardian dog of the dead appears in many cultures; Hindu tradition has Yama's two four-eyed dogs.
could: Multi-headed animals do occur rarely (polycephaly), but they rarely survive long.
summary: A giant dog with three heads (Hesiod says fifty), a serpent tail and snakes growing from its back. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).

name: Sphinx
first: Great Sphinx of Giza (c. 2500 BCE); Greek sphinx in Hesiod (c. 700 BCE)
looks: Egyptian: a lion with a human (pharaoh's) head. Greek: a lion's body, eagle's wings and a woman's head.
habitat: Egyptian sphinxes guard temples and tombs; the Greek Sphinx sat on a rock outside Thebes.
diet: The Greek Sphinx ate travellers who failed her riddle.
powers: The Greek Sphinx posed a riddle: 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening?'
stories: Oedipus answered 'Man' — crawling as a baby, walking as an adult, using a cane in old age — and the Sphinx threw herself from her rock. The reward, marriage to Thebes' widowed queen, led to Oedipus's tragedy.
belief: In Egypt sphinxes were protective symbols of royal power; the Great Sphinx probably has Khafre's face.
could: No, but the Great Sphinx was carved from a natural limestone outcrop.
connections: Ancient Egypt; Old Kingdom of Egypt; Greek religion and mythology; Great Pyramid built

name: Basilisk
first: Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77 CE)
looks: A small serpent with a crown-like mark; medieval versions became a rooster-serpent (cockatrice).
habitat: The deserts of Cyrenaica (Libya).
powers: Kills with its gaze and breath; scorches grass and splits rocks.
stories: Pliny says only the weasel's odour can kill it. Medieval legends said a basilisk hatched from a rooster's egg incubated by a toad, and could be killed by seeing its reflection.
belief: Feared through the Middle Ages; Harry Potter revived it.
could: No. Its legend may be based on cobras, which spit venom and raise hoods like crowns. The real basilisk lizard of Central America, which runs on water, is named after it.
summary: A small serpent with a crown-like mark; medieval versions became a rooster-serpent (cockatrice). First attested: Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77 CE).

name: Dragon
first: Mesopotamian serpent-dragons such as the mušḫuššu (from c. 2100 BCE) and Tiamat in the Enuma Elish; Greek drakon from Homer; medieval fire-breathing dragon in Beowulf (c. 700–1000 CE)
looks: A giant winged reptile with four legs, scales, claws and fiery breath (in medieval Europe).
habitat: Caves, mountains and treasure hoards; also lakes and the sea.
diet: Livestock, maidens offered as tribute, and treasure-hunters.
powers: Fire breath, flight, poisonous blood, near-impenetrable scales; dragon's blood or heart could give invulnerability or understanding of birds.
stories: The Babylonian god Marduk slays the chaos dragon Tiamat to create the world. In Greek myth Apollo kills the Python at Delphi, and a dragon guards the Golden Fleece for Jason. Beowulf dies killing a dragon that guards a treasure hoard. Sigurd kills the dragon Fáfnir and bathes in its blood. In the 13th-century Golden Legend, Saint George kills a dragon that demanded a princess as sacrifice in Libya — the image on England's flag-saint tradition.
belief: European dragons symbolised chaos, greed and evil (the devil in Revelation is a 'great red dragon'). The red dragon became the emblem of Wales.
could: Not as fire-breathing flying giants: no animal produces fire, and a huge four-legged reptile with wings would have six limbs. But fossils of dinosaurs and huge reptiles likely encouraged belief, and real 'dragons' exist: the Komodo dragon (up to 3 m) and the gliding Draco lizards. The bombardier beetle sprays boiling chemicals — the closest thing to 'fire' in nature.
verdict: Impossible as described — fossils likely fuelled the legend
slayers: Saint George, Sigurd, Beowulf, Marduk, Apollo, Jason (subdued)
connections: Mesopotamian religion; Greek religion and mythology; Norse religion; Christianity; Beowulf; Saint George; Sigurd; Beowulf manuscript

name: Leviathan
first: Ugaritic Baal Cycle (c. 1400 BCE) as Lotan; Hebrew Bible (Job 41, Psalm 74, Isaiah 27:1)
looks: A colossal sea serpent or dragon with impenetrable scales and fiery breath (Job 41).
habitat: The depths of the sea.
diet: Unspecified; it symbolises chaos rather than a hunter.
powers: Unbeatable by humans — 'Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook?' (Job 41:1).
stories: In the Ugaritic texts, the storm god Baal defeats Lotan, the seven-headed serpent; the Hebrew Bible says God crushed the heads of Leviathan and will slay it at the end of days. Jewish legend says its flesh will be served at a feast for the righteous.
belief: Thomas Hobbes used it as the title of his 1651 book on the all-powerful state. The word now means anything enormous.
could: No sea serpent of that kind exists, though whales and crocodiles probably inspired it. Palaeontologists named a giant fossil predatory whale Livyatan melvillei, which hunted whales 12 million years ago.
verdict: Mythical — inspired by whales and crocodiles
connections: Judaism; Ancient Israel and Judah; Christianity; Ugaritic

name: Djinn (Jinn)
first: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetry and belief; the Quran (7th century CE), especially Surah al-Jinn (72)
looks: Invisible beings who can take human or animal form; in folklore, ghostly shapes of smoke or fire.
habitat: Deserts, ruins, wells, cemeteries and a parallel unseen world; in stories, bottles and lamps.
diet: In some traditions, bones and dung; Islamic tradition says jinn eat and drink.
powers: Shape-shifting, invisibility, great strength, travel at enormous speed; some are believers and some evil (shayatin).
stories: The Quran says jinn were created from 'smokeless fire', have free will and will be judged. King Solomon (Sulaiman) commanded jinn to build for him. The One Thousand and One Nights is full of jinn granting wishes and trapped in bottles; 'Aladdin', with the genie of the lamp, was added by the French translator Antoine Galland in 1710 from a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab.
belief: For many Muslims, jinn are part of religious belief rather than folklore; exorcism (ruqyah) is practised. In the West, the 'genie' became a comic wish-granter.
could: Science cannot test claims about invisible beings; for believers this is a matter of faith. Folklorists note jinn beliefs often explain illness, bad luck and fears of desolate places.
summary: Invisible beings who can take human or animal form; in folklore, ghostly shapes of smoke or fire. First attested: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetry and belief; the Quran (7th century CE), especially Surah al-Jinn (72).

name: Golem
first: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b (c. 5th century CE): the sage Rava creates a man; Sefer Yetzirah; Prague legend from the 19th century
looks: A human figure made of clay or mud.
habitat: Wherever its creator needs it; the Prague golem is said to lie in the attic of the Old New Synagogue.
diet: None — it does not eat or speak.
powers: Great strength and obedience; brought to life with a holy name or the word 'emet' (truth) on its forehead; erasing the first letter to make 'met' (death) deactivates it.
stories: In the best-known legend, Rabbi Judah Loew (the Maharal) of Prague created a golem in the 16th century to protect the Jewish ghetto from antisemitic attacks. When it grew too powerful, he deactivated it. The story was popularised in the 19th century.

name: Yeti
first: Sherpa folklore; 'metoh-kangmi' mistranslated as 'Abominable Snowman' after the 1921 Everest expedition
looks: A large ape-like creature covered in hair.
habitat: High Himalayan snowfields and forests.
diet: Yaks and small animals.
powers: Elusive.
stories: Eric Shipton photographed a large footprint in 1951. Monasteries kept 'yeti scalps'. In 2019 the Indian Army posted photos of giant footprints near Makalu.
belief: Central to Sherpa and Tibetan folklore.
could: A 2017 DNA study of 'yeti' hair, bones and teeth found they came from Himalayan brown bears, Asian black bears and a dog. The extinct giant ape Gigantopithecus lived in southern China until about 300,000 years ago.

name: Wendigo
first: Algonquian peoples' oral traditions (Ojibwe, Cree, Innu); recorded by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century
looks: A gaunt, ice-hearted giant, always hungry.
habitat: Northern forests in winter.
diet: Human flesh; it grows larger the more it eats, so is never satisfied.
powers: A person who resorts to cannibalism can become a wendigo.
stories: In 1879 the Cree man Swift Runner was executed after killing and eating his family during a famine, claiming possession by a wendigo.
belief: A warning against greed and cannibalism in times of starvation.
could: No. 'Wendigo psychosis' was described by anthropologists as a culture-bound syndrome, but some argue it was largely a colonial construct.
summary: A gaunt, ice-hearted giant, always hungry. First attested: Algonquian peoples' oral traditions (Ojibwe, Cree, Innu); recorded by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century.

name: Mermaid
first: Syrian goddess Atargatis, depicted half-fish (c. 1st millennium BCE); Greek sirens were originally bird-women
looks: Upper body of a woman, tail of a fish.
habitat: The sea.
diet: Fish; some lure sailors.
powers: Enchanting songs; storms.
stories: Christopher Columbus reported seeing three 'mermaids' in 1493, but noted they were not as pretty as pictured — almost certainly manatees. P. T. Barnum exhibited the 'Feejee Mermaid' in 1842, a monkey sewn to a fish. Hans Christian Andersen wrote The Little Mermaid (1837).
belief: Mami Wata in African traditions, Matsya (Vishnu's fish avatar).
could: No. In 2012 the US NOAA stated there is no evidence of mermaids. Manatees and dugongs likely inspired sightings.
